analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and lowers top income and corporate tax rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from January 2009 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made the Bush-era tax cuts from 2001 and 2003 permanent instead of letting them expire as scheduled. It also would have temporarily cut every individual income tax rate for 2009 through 2014 — including dropping the top rate from 35% to 25% — and cut the corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25%. Middle-class provisions like lower rates on the first dollars earned, a tuition deduction, and bigger small-business equipment expensing were bundled in. It was referred to the tax-writing committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and profitable corporations gain the most: the bill makes permanent the lowered rates on capital gains and dividends, drops the top individual rate to 25%, and cuts the corporate rate to 25%. Middle-income taxpayers gain smaller per-dollar amounts from the reduced 10%, 15%, and 25% rates, and small businesses gain from a permanent $125,000 equipment-expensing allowance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, corporations, and small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the 2001 tax cuts and the 2003 reductions in dividend and capital gains tax rates, which were otherwise scheduled to expire after 2010.
Cuts each individual income tax rate for 2009-2014: the 10% and 15% rates each drop by 5 percentage points, and the top rates fall from 25% to 20%, 28% to 23%, and both 33% and 35% to 25%.
Cuts the corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25% for 2009-2014.
Makes permanent the deduction for state and local sales taxes and the deduction for tuition and related expenses.
Raises the small-business expensing allowance for equipment to $125,000 permanently, with the phaseout starting at $500,000 in investment.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers collectively, through larger deficits: making the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent removes their scheduled expiration, which was the mechanism that had held down their long-term cost. Because the largest rate reductions fall on the top brackets and corporate income, the revenue given up is concentrated at the top, while any future spending cuts or taxes to close the gap fall broadly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal revenues, through trillions in added deficits

drawbacks.text: Permanently extending the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts was the single largest driver of projected deficits; the sunsets in those laws existed precisely to keep their official 10-year cost down, and repealing them would add on the order of trillions to deficits over a decade (general knowledge; the Congressional Budget Office scored the original sunsets in the trillions).

The largest cuts go to the top of the income scale: collapsing the 33% and 35% brackets into 25% is a 24-29% rate cut for the highest earners, while cutting 15% to 10% is a smaller per-dollar gain and helps people with tax liability in the first place.
Cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 25% primarily benefits shareholders and profitable large firms, and the bill includes no offsetting revenue.

The bill was introduced two weeks after a Democratic landslide gave the opposing party large House and Senate majorities, with no negotiation across the aisle, which limited its realistic prospects from the start.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Middle-class taxpayers would have gotten real but modest help: lower rates on their income brackets, a permanent tuition deduction, and a sales-tax deduction. But the bill's cost is dominated by the permanent extension of tax cuts that disproportionately benefit the highest earners and by a 10-point corporate rate cut, all unpaid for. Weighing the middle-class provisions against the size and concentration of the revenue loss, the design is a top-heavy tax cut with middle-class provisions attached, not a balanced stimulus package.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Neugebauer introduced the bill on January 8, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax legislation.
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled, and the full House never considered the bill.
47 of the 178 House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
The Congress ended January 3, 2011, without the bill ever reaching a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one received the bill's tax cuts, so federal revenue was spared the large permanent rate reductions for the top brackets and corporations. High-income households and profitable corporations lost the chance at those lower rates; middle-income taxpayers never saw the proposed cuts to their rates either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue; taxpayers got no cuts

for.name: Rep. Randy Neugebauer
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 8, 2009 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Charles Rangel (D-NY) in 2009
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral on January 8, 2009; never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: 253-member House Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committee schedule and floor calendar and never brought the bill to a vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 47 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; the Democratic House majority never acted on the bill, so support was entirely one-party while opposition took the form of inaction rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have made the reduced capital gains and dividend rates permanent and cut the top individual rate from 35% to 25%. Its largest dollar benefits flow to the top of the income distribution, and the revenue given up is the public's cost.
A 10-point corporate rate cut from 35% to 25% would have gone straight to corporate bottom lines and shareholders, with no offsetting revenue in the bill.

The permanent $125,000 equipment-expensing allowance lets small firms deduct equipment costs immediately rather than over years, a straightforward cash-flow benefit that does not come at ordinary people's expense except through the overall deficit.

Permanent low rates on dividends and capital gains support the market for investment products these firms sell, and the bill names financial services among its subjects; the benefit accrues to their clients and balance sheets.
